newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian firms seen eyeing best of state oil stakes.
newsitem.headline: Russian firms seen eyeing best of state oil stakes.

text.p: Russia said on Wednesday it will start selling state stakes in six oil firms early next month, and Russia's nascent private energy sector will be looking for strategic fits among a mixed bag of assets, oil analysts said.

Privatisation Minister Alfred Kokh said on Russian radio that the auctions, originally scheduled to start on June 19, would begin in early July and could net the government between $700 million and $1 billion.

"Russia's Federal Property Fund and the Fuel and Energy Ministry have agreed the schedule of auctions for six Russian oil companies, which I think will be declared in early July," he told the Ekho-Moskvy radio station.

The six companies are -- Tyumenskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (Tyumen Oil Co), OAO Vostochnaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (Eastern Oil), Norsi-Oil, AO KomiTEK, Vostochno-Sibirskaya Neftegazovaya Kompaniya (Vostsibneftegaz) and Sibirsko-Uralskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (Sibur).
The volume of state stakes in the six companies to be auctioned has yet to be announced.
Analysts said the prize assets of the list are Tyumen Oil and Norsi-Oil.

Tyumen Oil is the fifth or sixth biggest oil company in Russia by output, producing 21.30 million tonnes (426,000 barrels per day) of oil in 1996, six percent down on 1995. It plans to produce 20.13 million tonnes (402,600 bpd) this year.
But it is not without its problems.

The government recently filed bankruptcy proceedings against Tyumen's main production unit, Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, in a move some analysts said would allow the state to appoint managers more sympathetic to its energy policy.
"The government has had enough," Ivan Mazalov of CentreInvest Securities in Moscow. "The company has needed an overhaul for a long time and there needs to be some change."
Bankruptcy proceedings could also decrease competition in any auction or tender, making life easier for the firm some analysts see as a probable bidder, the Central Fuel Company.
"The Central Fuel Company will probably want to take a stake in Nizhnevartovskneftegaz," an analyst said.
The CFC, based in the political heartland of Moscow, is a refining and trading operation, and may be looking to establish its own production base, he added.
Tyumen's attraction for investors depends on the fate of its giant Samotlor oil field, one of Russia's largest.
The field needs major investment to increase output and decrease costs, and its fate depends on whether the field could be developed under production-sharing terms, analysts said.

Samotlor is one of a list of seven mineral and hydrocarbon reserves qualifying for development under production sharing agreements passed by the lower parliament State Duma earlier this week, but is not open to foreign investment.
"Samotlor can be resurrected, but it is going to need some considerable investment," the analyst said.

The most clear-cut of the auctions appears to be Norsi-Oil, one of Russia's largest refineries processing around 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude. LUKoil already has a stake in the company and is heavily backed to win the stake.
"For LUKoil, obviously Norsi is a priority," said Aleksei Kokin, oil and gas analyst at Renaissance Capital.

LUKoil has promised to invest in upgrading Norsi, the acquisition of which would be consistent with its drive to boost refining capacity and export more value-added products. LUKoil plans to supply 200,000 bpd of crude to the plant.
Of the remaining four companies, Eastern Oil is the most alluring, analysts said.

"Eastern Oil has some interesting acreage and refining capacity that may be sought by Sibneft NYGS.RTS, although there could be a conflict of interest in the products distribution and marketing arms," said one.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said LUKoil might also bid for Eastern Oil in its search for increased production and reserves.
Eastern Oil produced 11.2 million tonnes (224,000 bpd) in 1996, little changed from 1995 levels.

KomiTEK produced 3.26 million tonnes of oil (65,200 bpd) in 1996, excluding joint venture output, down from 5.17 million (103,400 bpd) in 1995. Its Ukhta refinery is small, processed 61,000 bpd of oil in 1996, according to industry estimates.
Vostsibneftegaz produced 11,400 tonnes (228 bpd) in 1996.
Sibur does produce oil, but refines gas to produce chemical products, a company source said.
